CANShield: multiple CNN-based autoencoders working on signal-level CAN time-series views, with ensemble-based detection.
Yes. It is designed to run onboard or on a gateway/OBD-II-connected device for near real-time detection.

No.

Accuracy / detection performance, responsiveness, false positives, detection latency.

Journal article (IEEE Access)

Build a frame-by-frame (not block/period-based) CAN IDS using multi-observation Hidden Markov Models over both the ID and data-field domains, to detect anomalies without needing extensive labeled attack data and to precisely localize which single frame is malicious rather than just flagging an attack period.

In-vehicle CAN bus; real vehicle CAN data collected via a custom-built RS465 CAN HAT + Raspberry Pi transceiver through OBD-II, plus a custom CAN bus attack platform (real vehicle instrumentation system + gateway) used to physically inject attacks.

Four attack scenarios explicitly defined and tested: DDoS attack, Fuzzy attack, Replay attack (split into reply_invariant and reply_variant), and Masquerade attack. Masquerade attacks ARE explicitly covered: the attacker replaces specific normal frame data fields with target control information (e.g., to trigger wipers, brakes, or steering) while IDs and data fields stay within the legal range.

Own real-vehicle dataset: normal data collected from a car driving normally for 30 minutes during non-peak hours in an urban area (31 real CAN IDs); attacks generated on their own built CAN bus attack platform (real vehicle instrumentation system + gateway).
Real: real vehicle CAN traffic for normal data, and real physically-injected attacks via their own hardware attack platform on a real vehicle instrumentation system (not purely simulated/synthetic).

Multiple-Observation Hidden Markov Model: one HMM per data-field byte (L HMMs total), using the ID sequence as HMM states and each byte of the data field as an observation sequence; computes forward-backward probabilities (gamma) per frame per time window and flags a frame abnormal if gamma falls outside a learned threshold range for any byte.
Yes — a lightweight, frame-by-frame onboard detection algorithm requiring no changes to existing vehicle architecture.

Explainable Edge-Cloud Federated Intrusion Detection System for Electric Vehicles Using GRUs, DRL Selection, and Integrated Gradients
Arash Heidari, Seyed Hamed Rastegar, Ahmad Khonsari
Journal article (Journal of Big Data, Springer) — Accepted manuscript / 'Article in Press' (accepted 12 July 2026, published online 12 Aug 2026).

Build a scalable, real-time, privacy-preserving, energy-aware, and EXPLAINABLE intrusion detection system for Internet of Electric Vehicles (IoEV), addressing gaps in prior federated IDS work: no energy-aware participant selection, fixed (non-adaptive) learning schedules, limited explainability/auditability, weak edge-cloud hierarchical coordination, and treating detection and learning as separate rather than adaptive processes.

Three-tier IoEV/V2X hierarchy: EV On-Board Units/Telematics Control Units (vehicle layer) -> Charging-Hub Edge (CHE)/Roadside Unit nodes (edge layer) -> centralized vehicular cloud (cloud layer), connected via C-V2X (PC5/Uu) links and a high-speed 5G/fiber backhaul between edge and cloud.

V2X-level communication attacks: spoofing, tampering/message manipulation, and replay of V2X beacons/telemetry (e.g., a rogue edge/CHE node intercepting and manipulating vehicle-edge traffic). This is telemetry/V2X-level threat detection, NOT CAN-bus frame-level masquerade attacks — no CAN ID/payload masquerade concept as defined in the ROAD-dataset literature is used here.

Seven benchmark datasets: ToN-IoT, Car-Hacking and CAN-intrusion datasets (raw CAN traffic + injection attacks), CICIDS2017, CSE-CIC-IDS2018, UNSW-NB15, and VeReMi (V2X misbehavior and location-spoofing simulation). Does NOT use the ROAD dataset.

Mixed: public benchmark datasets (real captured network/CAN/V2X data) partitioned into simulated federated EV clients (non-IID via Dirichlet distributions); supplemented with real Hardware-in-the-Loop validation (Raspberry Pi 4 / ARM Cortex-A72 OBU-grade board) and a Field-in-the-Loop pilot replaying real CAN/GPS/aux-sensor logs with injected drift and zero-day behavior.

Lightweight GRU-based IDS (2xGRU layers, input sequence length T=10, H=64 hidden units) running locally on each EV over 1-second telemetry windows; a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DQN) agent at each CHE node for EV participant SELECTION (not detection); FedAvg-style hierarchical federated aggregation across CHE and cloud tiers; Integrated Gradients (IG) for on-device, post-hoc explainability of each alert.
Yes — the GRU IDS itself runs on the EV OBU/TCU, processing 1-second telemetry windows locally in real time.

NO in the sense our project cares about: the cloud does NOT run a second, independent detection model that re-examines individual alerts. The cloud's role is federated-learning aggregation and global model refinement only — it never re-scores a specific EV's suspicious frame with a stronger model.

Yes, but only of MODEL UPDATES/TRAINING, never of individual detection decisions: model weight updates flow EV -> CHE -> cloud -> back down; raw telemetry and per-alert inference never leave the EV. This is fundamentally different from offloading an uncertain alert itself for cloud confirmation.

CRITICAL CLARIFICATION: 'DRL Selection' in the title refers to the CHE choosing WHICH EVs get to participate in each FEDERATED TRAINING round (based on energy budget, link quality/SNR, State-of-Charge, compute availability, and data-quality contribution, cast as an MDP with a DQN agent) — it does NOT decide whether a specific suspicious CAN/V2X frame should be escalated to the cloud for a second opinion before an alert deadline. There is no per-alert escalation decision anywhere in this paper.

Yes — extensively, but as system/network engineering conditions, not as an alert-escalation criterion: DSRC/C-V2X latency jitter (mu=20-80ms, sigma=10-30ms) and random RSU dropout (p=0.05-0.20) are used as realistic stress conditions for federated convergence and energy measurements.

No explicit named 'alert deadline' policy variable, though the paper does target and report real-time in-vehicle alerting: end-to-end alert latency has a median of approx. 250ms and 95th percentile under 400ms in the Field-in-the-Loop pilot, described as 'achieving the real-time condition for in-vehicle alerting' -- this is a reported outcome, not a decision-time deadline constraint used to decide whether to query the cloud.

Window-level: 1-second (Delta t = 1s) sliding windows per EV form the GRU's input sequences (fixed length T=10 timesteps); detection/alert decisions are per-window, not per discrete CAN masquerade event in the ROAD-dataset sense.

Four federated IDS baselines: FGID (federated GAN-based IDS), FSLD (federated semi-supervised IDS with teacher-student networks), FCBR (Fed-CALiBER, a federated lightweight BERT model over CAN bus data), and EFFX (an Explainable Federated Framework for APT detection using SHAP).

Accuracy (up to 99.2% / 96.2% under IID), F1-score (98.7% / 95.7%), ROC-AUC (0.981), PR-AUC (0.974), energy per round/per decision/total lifecycle training energy (25-38% reduction vs. baselines), convergence rounds (R95, 30-50 rounds faster), resilience and redistribution-efficiency scores under RSU/cloud failure, cross-domain transfer F1/AUC/accuracy-drop, IG attribution fidelity (91%), and end-to-end alert latency.

Real, meaningful overlaps: (1) a hierarchical EV(local)-edge-cloud IDS architecture; (2) realistic communication delay/dropout (DSRC/C-V2X jitter, RSU dropout) treated as first-class evaluation conditions rather than ignored; (3) explicit end-to-end alert-latency CDF reporting, which is close to the kind of timing evidence a deadline-based framework would need to justify a deadline budget; (4) a GRU-based local temporal detector, similar in spirit to several CAN-focused papers elsewhere in this table.

CRUCIALLY: despite the title mentioning 'DRL Selection' and 'Edge-Cloud', this is NOT a per-alert cloud-confirmation/escalation architecture (see column P). It targets general IoEV/V2X telemetry threats using non-CAN-masquerade datasets (ToN-IoT, CICIDS2017, CSE-CIC-IDS2018, UNSW-NB15, VeReMi) rather than CAN-bus masquerade attacks specifically, and does not use the ROAD dataset. There is no false-alarm-budget-conditioned, deadline-gated decision to query a stronger cloud model for a specific uncertain case.

Does not perform deadline-aware, per-case cloud escalation for detection confirmation; does not address CAN-bus masquerade attacks specifically (its 'spoofing/tampering' attacks operate at the V2X/telemetry level, not within CAN frame ID/payload semantics the way ROAD-style masquerade attacks do); does not use the ROAD dataset or any CAN-masquerade-specific benchmark.

Explicitly listed by the authors as future work: (1) cryptographic privacy hardening (secure aggregation / differential privacy) against eavesdropping and poisoning; (2) adaptive/continual online learning for long-term drift; (3) blockchain / secure-identity integration to eliminate rogue edge (CHE) nodes; (4) post-quantum-secure federated coordination for future qIoV; (5) global reward shaping or meta-learning to help the DRL participant-selection policy generalize to unseen fleets/vehicle types.

This paper is NOT the novelty threat it appeared to be from the title alone. 'DRL Selection' is federated-learning CLIENT selection (an energy/data-quality optimization for who trains this round), not a decision policy about whether to escalate an individual detection case to a cloud-side confirmation model under a deadline -- which remains our project's specific, undiscussed niche. It IS, however, a strong related-architecture reference worth citing for its hierarchical EV-edge-cloud structure and its rigorous treatment of real communication latency/dropout and end-to-end alert timing.

It is IoEV/V2X-general (7 non-CAN-masquerade datasets) rather than CAN-masquerade-specific, and does not use ROAD. Cite it for the hierarchical architecture and realistic latency/dropout evaluation methodology (useful template for our own evaluation design), and explicitly state in our related-work section how our per-alert, deadline-gated cloud-confirmation policy differs from its per-round, energy-aware client-selection policy.
